an3.65:1.1: This is a key text in understanding Buddhist modernism, as 20th century teachers often cited it as a Buddhist “charter of free inquiry”. Its teachings are not unusual, but the context has a modern resonance: how to present the teachings to a skeptical audience, weary of different teachings. | The discourse is usually named Kālāmasutta today, but the colophons typically name it _kesaputtiyā_, “the Kesiyans”. The variant _kesamuttiyā_ would mean “those of loosed hair” and seems unlikely. The title in the MS edition, _kesamuttisutta_, appears to be an unwarranted abridgment of the variant.
an3.65:1.2: The Kālāmas are hardly attested in ancient literature, being remembered only here and as the clan of Āḷāra ([mn26:15.1]()) and Bharaṇḍu ([an3.126:3.3]()). | The town of Kesaputta is likewise poorly attested. It perhaps modern Kesariya, where there is a large ancient Buddhist monument. Its people are perhaps the Keśins whose troubled rites of kingship are recorded in Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 11.8.4, and who were possibly descended from Keśin Dālbhya, a founding king of the Pañcāla realm (see J.P. Sharma. *Republics in Ancient India*, pp. 231–6). They were a small republic of democratic governance, nestled between river Sarayū and the Mallakas to the north, the Ganges to the south, and Varanasi to the southwest. As this passage shows, by this time they had come under the sovereignty of the powerful Kosalan kingdom to the west, as had the Sakyans and the Bhaggas.
